groups.title: The three controls
questions: Q1a. 'I built and sold two companies before I was thirty.' — which control?
Q1b. 'Nine out of ten people who start one are still running it five years later.' — which control?
Q1c. 'Imagine never having to ask anyone for permission again.' — which control?

groups.title: Impact: the three-step chain
questions: Q2a. NAME IT — 'Imagine never having to ask anyone for permission again.'
Q2b. FEEL IT — what does that line do to the reader?
Q2c. WHY IT WORKS — why would a writer put that line where they put it?

groups.title: Fly it solo
questions: MASTERY Line A — NAME IT: 'Our need for human connection is like our need for food and water: essential for our survival.'
MASTERY Line A — FEEL IT: what does that line do to the reader?
MASTERY Line A — WHY IT WORKS: why is this line in the last paragraph and not the first?

MASTERY Line B — NAME IT: 'This work will take all of us: schools, workplaces, community organizations, government, health workers, public health professionals, individuals, families and more working together.'
MASTERY Line B — He could have written 'everyone' but wrote out the whole long list. What does the long list do to the reader, and why did he do it?

groups.title: Before you go
questions: EXIT TICKET Q1. How solid do you feel on describing the impact of rhetoric right now? (1-4)
EXIT TICKET Q2. In your own words, what does 'impact' mean when we're talking about rhetoric?

groups.title: Spot it in the wild
questions: HOMEWORK Q1. Which did you pick, and what exactly did they say?
HOMEWORK Q2. NAME IT — which control were they flying with?
HOMEWORK Q3. FEEL IT + WHY IT WORKS — what did it do to you, and why do you think they said it that way?

groups.title: About it, or aimed at it
questions: Q1. In Hurston's line “I remember the very day that I became colored,” one word is doing almost all of the work. Which one, and what does it do that a different word wouldn't?

groups.title: Swap the word, break the sentence
questions: Q2. Rewrite Douglass's line without the word “your,” then say in one sentence what the line lost.
Q3. Choosing either Orwell's line or Hurston's line: what is that essay probably aimed at (not what it is about), and which exact words got you there?

groups.title: Letters as mouth pictures
questions: Q1. Say mmm and nnn slowly and notice where each happens in your mouth. Looking at ㅁ and ㄴ — what is each shape showing you?
Q2. ㅗ and ㅜ are the same two pieces with the sun in a different place. Which is oh and which is oo, and what is the rule?

groups.title: The mirror pair
questions: Q3. Which mirror pair did you pick (ㅏ/ㅓ or ㅗ/ㅜ), and what changes in your mouth between them — lips, tongue, or jaw?

groups.title: Read five new words
questions: Q1a. 소미 (a singer's name) — how does it sound?
Q1b. 누나 (what a boy calls an older girl) — how does it sound?
Q1c. 가사 (lyrics) — how does it sound?
Q1d. 어머니 (mother) — how does it sound?
Q1e. 오이 (cucumber) — how does it sound?

groups.title: Same letters, different order
questions: Q2. 미소 (smile) and 소미 (a name) use the same three letters. Which letters go in which block for each word, and why does moving them change what you say?

groups.title: How sure are you
questions: Q3. On a scale of 1 to 4, how confident are you that you could read an unseen Korean syllable block out loud? What one thing would move you up by one?

groups.title: Spot one in the wild
questions: Q1. Pause a K-pop video or K-drama on Korean writing and find one letter you know. Which letter, and where did you see it?

groups.title: Read three blocks
questions: Q2a. How does 고 sound?
Q2b. How does 너 sound?
Q2c. How does 스 sound?

groups.title: What you can't read yet
questions: Q3. In 사랑 and 오빠 — which pieces can you read, and which can't you read yet?

groups.title: Spell three you already know
questions: Q1a. Write “singer” (ga-su) in Korean blocks.
Q1b. Write “tree” (na-mu) in Korean blocks.
Q1c. Write “cucumber” (o-i) in Korean blocks.
Q2. A block can never be a vowel sitting by itself. What is the circle in 오 actually for, and what would go wrong without it?

groups.title: Five letters you already half-know
questions: Q3. Pick any one of the five new letters. Cover the added stroke — say the letter that's left, then the new one. What changes in your mouth between them?
Q4. ㅇ makes no sound; ㅎ is the same circle with two strokes on top and makes a real h. What do you think extra strokes are for in this alphabet?

groups.title: Read five you have never seen
questions: Q1a. 두부 (tofu) — how does it sound?
Q1b. 머리 (head / hair) — how does it sound?
Q1c. 호수 (a lake) — how does it sound?
Q1d. 바지 (pants) — how does it sound?
Q1e. 도시 (a city) — how does it sound?

groups.title: Now write three back
questions: Q2a. Write “a sound” (so-ri) in Korean blocks.
Q2b. Write “a rich person” (bu-ja) in Korean blocks.
Q2c. Write “one day” (ha-ru) in Korean blocks.

groups.title: Look at what that was
questions: Q3. Which was harder — reading the five words, or writing the three? Why?
Q4. 1 to 4 — how sure are you that you could read an unseen Korean block with no chart? What one thing would move you up by one?

groups.title: Ten words — do you know them
questions: Q1a. 나비 — what does it mean?
Q1b. 머리 — what does it mean?
Q1c. 우리 — what does it mean?
Q1d. 사자 — what does it mean?
Q1e. 다리 — what does it mean?

groups.title: Write four of them back
questions: Q2a. Write “one” (ha-na) in Korean blocks.
Q2b. Write “butterfly” (na-bi) in Korean blocks.
Q2c. Write “we / us / our” (u-ri) in Korean blocks.
Q2d. Write “lion” (sa-ja) in Korean blocks.

groups.title: Put two of them somewhere real
questions: Q3. Pick two words from the ten. Where would you actually run into each one?
Q4. Find one of the five new letters (ㄷ ㄹ ㅂ ㅈ ㅎ) somewhere Korean in the wild. Which letter, and where?

groups.title: Part 1 — The case
questions: What is the narrator hiding? Four candidate answers, five clues released one at a time. The student commits whenever they choose; the page records how many clues they used and whether they were right, then replays every clue showing what it ruled out.

groups.title: Part 2 — The evidence
questions: Q1. Which single clue was the strongest? Quote it and say what it rules out.
Q2. Which clue can honestly be read two ways? Give both readings and say which you would defend.

groups.title: Part 3 — Close it
questions: Q1. In two sentences: the answer, and the exact words that prove it.
Q2. Was there a moment you were sure and then changed your mind? What did it, and what did you think before?

groups.title: Part 1 — Paint it dark
questions: Using only word swaps in four slots, move a neutral hallway sentence all the way into the DREAD zone. No events may be added.

groups.title: Part 2 — Now paint it calm
questions: Same sentence, opposite direction: move it all the way into the CALM zone. Ends with both versions shown side by side and a bar chart of how far each chosen word pulled.

groups.title: Part 3 — Your call
questions: New sentence (the water and the shore). The student chooses the target zone — CALM, UNEASY or DREAD — then has to land it. UNEASY is deliberately the hardest.

groups.title: Part 4 — Say what you did
questions: Q1. Which single word moved the sentence furthest, and what does it do to the reader?
Q2. In Part 2 you calmed the sentence without deleting any event — so where was the fear actually coming from?
Q3. Write a flat sentence about something ordinary, then repaint it so it feels wrong, changing nothing but the words.

groups.title: Part 1 — The sprint
questions: A sixty-second retrieval round on one of four decks — Gothic devices, ethos/pathos/logos, Hangul letters to sounds, or discussion moves. One prompt at a time, three options, wrong cards return to the queue. Repeatable; every round is recorded.

groups.title: Part 2 — The ones that got away
questions: Q1. Pick one you missed and write down something that will make it stick.
Q2. Which one did you get right but have to think about?

groups.title: Part 1 — Spot the move
questions: For each of five real nonfiction lines (Orwell, King, Douglass, Hurston ×2): which move is the writer making — the Pile-Up, the Loaded Word, the Question That Isn't a Question, or the Two Pictures?

groups.title: Part 2 — What it does to you
questions: For each line: what does this move actually do to the reader? Choose from seven effects; two belong to none of the lines.

groups.title: Part 3 — Aim it at something bigger
questions: For each line: which universal idea is it aimed at — Power, Justice, Belonging, or Identity? (Orwell's line accepts either Power or Justice if backed.)

groups.title: Part 4 — Your turn
questions: Q1. Which move did you use, and what bigger idea are you aiming at?
Q2. Your lines. Two to six of them — however many the thing needs.
Q3. Point at the exact word or phrase in your own writing that's doing the most work, and say what it does.

groups.title: Part 1 — The room
questions: Three turns of persuasion in front of six stakeholders with different starting positions and different reasons to care. Every choice changes every face and the state carries forward, so a person driven to 'against you' is dug in and only a concession-type move can reach them. Appeal names (ethos / pathos / logos) are revealed only after all three turns.

groups.title: Part 2 — Read the room back
questions: Q1. Who was hardest to win over, and what exact sentence would you have said to them?
Q2. Which line helped one person and cost another? Name both, and say whether it was worth it.
Q3. One move did not try to win the argument. What was it doing instead, and why does that reach somebody the other kind cannot? (challenge:+1 item — flagged as meant to be hard)

groups.title: Part 1 — Terror or horror?
questions: For each of six one-line Gothic scenes: is this terror (it has not happened yet, you cannot see it) or horror (it has happened, it is in front of you)? One line is deliberately arguable and accepts either answer.

groups.title: Part 2 — Name the move
questions: For each of four lines: which device is doing the work — personification, hyperbole, foreshadowing, or motif?

groups.title: Part 3 — Your turn
questions: Q1. The arguable line goes both ways. Pick a side — terror or horror — and say how you know.
Q2a. Thumbnail title text for A — makes people click because they're scared of what's in it (terror).
Q2b. Thumbnail title text for B — makes them click because of something they can already see (horror).
Q3. One sentence using a device of your choice to make a room full of people at a party feel wrong.
Q3b. Which device that sentence uses.
